item.title: Artemis III Mission to feature live 4K video powered by Starlink lasers - SpaceQ
item.description:
NASA has tapped SpaceX to upgrade the communication capabilities of the Artemis III mission scheduled for next year. NASA will install two Starlink mini laser terminals on the exterior of the Orion spacecraft. This hardware will allow astronauts to send 4K video and high-resolution imagery back to the Mission Control Center in Houston.

For the public, this means unprecedented access to the mission. During the 2027 flight, four astronauts will test how Orion approaches and docks with the commercial lunar landing systems required to return humans to the Moon in 2028. Viewers on Earth will be able to watch these tests unfold in real-time detail.

The integrated Starlink terminals use optical communications. Instead of relying on traditional radio waves, this system uses invisible infrared light. Shifting to optical wavelengths allows the equipment to handle much higher frequencies. This change vastly expands the available bandwidth, letting the spacecraft send large amounts of data and complex telemetry back to Earth far faster than legacy radio systems.

According to the a NASA update, the agency aims to “provide a front row seat for viewers from the Orion spacecraft” as the astronauts carry out their objectives. The new hardware will supplement the existing radio communication systems onboard Orion.

This is not the first time NASA has used light to talk to spacecraft. The agency successfully tested a similar laser system during the Artemis II mission. That test proved the equipment could send high-definition video, photos, and voice communications when the spacecraft had a direct, unobstructed line of sight with ground receivers on Earth.

SpaceX brings relevant experience to the project. The company demonstrated its laser technology for NASA during a 2025 spaceflight. The new hardware outfitting the Orion capsule for its low-Earth orbit demonstration flight is based on the same technology powering the more than 25,000 laser links currently connecting the Starlink internet satellites in orbit. SpaceX has already used this network to stream live video during its own Starship rocket tests.

The integration of these terminals is part of the Communications Services Project run by NASA’s Space Communications and Navigation division. This partnership helps NASA shift toward using commercial satellite services for missions close to Earth, freeing up government resources for deep space exploration.

item.title: NASA Outlines Preliminary Artemis III Mission Plans - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA is moving quickly to define next year’s Artemis III mission in Earth orbit, a crewed flight that will test rendezvous and docking capabilities between the agency’s Orion spacecraft and commercial landers from Blue Origin and SpaceX. Since a February announcement adding an Artemis mission ahead of crewed landing missions to the Moon’s South Pole region, engineers have been evaluating mission profile options and operational considerations for Artemis III to ensure the test flight helps the agency and its partners reduce risk ahead of the next Americans landing on the Moon during Artemis IV.

“While this is a mission to Earth orbit, it is an important stepping stone to successfully landing on the Moon with Artemis IV. Artemis III is one of the most highly complex missions NASA has undertaken,” said Jeremy Parsons, Moon to Mars acting assistant deputy administrator, NASA’s Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate in Washington. “For the first time, NASA will coordinate a launch campaign involving multiple spacecraft integrating new capabilities into Artemis operations. We’re integrating more partners and interrelated operations into this mission by design, which will help us learn how Orion, the crew, and ground teams all interact together with hardware and teams from both providers before we send astronauts to the Moon’s surface and build a Moon Base there.”

The mission is planned to carry out a series of objectives designed to demonstrate critical systems needed for a future lunar landing. During the Artemis III mission, the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket will launch the Orion spacecraft from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida with four crew members. Instead of using the interim cryogenic propulsion stage as the upper stage of the rocket, NASA will use a “spacer,” a representation of the mass and overall dimensions of an upper stage but without propulsive capabilities. The spacer will maintain the same overall dimensions and interface connection points as the upper stage between the Orion stage adapter and launch vehicle stage adapter.

Design and fabrication activities for the spacer are progressing rapidly at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Material for the barrel section and the upper and lower rings is currently being machined at Marshall in preparation for upcoming welding operations.

After the rocket delivers Orion to orbit, the spacecraft’s European-built service module will provide propulsion to circularize Orion’s orbit around the planet in low Earth orbit. This orbit increases overall mission success by allowing more launch opportunities for each element as compared to a lunar mission — SLS carrying Orion and its crew, SpaceX’s Starship human landing system pathfinder, and Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 human landing system pathfinder.

Informed by Blue Origin and SpaceX capabilities, NASA also is defining the concept of operations for the mission. While some decisions are yet to be determined, astronauts could potentially enter at least one lander test article.

The crew will spend more time aboard Orion than during Artemis II, further advancing the evaluation of life support systems, and for the first time will demonstrate the docking system performance. The mission will inform lander rendezvous and habitation concepts and mission operations in preparation for future surface missions. The agency also plans to test an upgraded heat shield during Orion’s return to Earth to enable more flexible and robust reentry profiles for future missions.

Over the coming weeks, NASA will continue to refine specific plans for the flight, including a timeline for identifying astronauts to train for mission operations, options to evaluate Axiom’s AxEMU spacesuit lander interfaces ahead of lunar surface missions, mission duration, and potential science operations for the flight. NASA has asked for industry input on potential solutions to improve the communications with the ground during the mission since the Deep Space Network will not be used. The agency also is seeking both international and domestic interest in potentially flying CubeSats to deploy in Earth orbit, and may share other opportunities as the concept of operations for the mission is further defined.

As part of the Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.

item.title: Shuttle-Era Engines Make Final Flight: RS-25s Delivered for Artemis III - Tech Times
item.description:
The last four rocket engines ever to fly with shuttle-era hardware at their core have arrived at NASA's Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans — and they are headed for the Moon program, not a museum.

L3Harris Technologies announced on July 22, 2026 that it completed delivery of four RS-25 main engines to Michoud, where they will be bolted vertically to the core stage of the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket for Artemis III. The delivery closes the shuttle-heritage chapter of American human spaceflight propulsion: every SLS launch from Artemis V onward will use newly manufactured engines built with modern additive manufacturing techniques, not hardware reclaimed from the shuttle program.

These Four Engines Already Have a History

The engines are not new. They carried astronauts and cargo across 36 Space Shuttle missions — a collective record that includes International Space Station assembly flights and the October 1998 return to space of Project Mercury astronaut and former Senator John Glenn aboard STS-95. Their serial numbers — E2048, E2052, E2054, and E2057 — trace back to a manufacturing era when each engine was expected to fly again and again, be refurbished, and fly again.

Reflight is what L3Harris did. For the first four Artemis missions, the company upgraded the engines with modern digital controllers and new thermal insulation rated for the more extreme environment of the SLS rocket, which runs the engines hotter than the shuttle ever did. During the shuttle program, the most demanding RS-25 operating condition called for 104.5 percent of the engine's original rated power level. SLS runs them at 109 percent. Together, four engines generating that output will produce more than 2 million pounds of thrust to send the Orion spacecraft and crew into orbit during Artemis III.

A New Way to Bolt an Engine to a Rocket

Beyond the engines themselves, the Artemis III integration introduces a procedural first. For all prior SLS missions, technicians installed the RS-25 engines while the core stage sat horizontally. For Artemis III, NASA and Boeing will integrate the engines with the core stage standing upright — the same orientation the rocket will hold on the launch pad.

The change is practical: a vertical stage gives technicians better access to each engine's mounting points, harnesses, and plumbing, and it eliminates a rotation step that previously required the assembled stage to be rotated before it could be stacked with the rest of the vehicle. L3Harris said the method will both simplify and accelerate the installation process.

Once integration is complete, Boeing and NASA technicians will conduct final checkout of the engine gimbaling systems — the mechanical actuators that let the engines steer the rocket by swiveling up to 8.5 degrees in any direction — before the 212-foot-tall (64.6-meter) core stage is loaded onto the Pegasus barge for delivery to Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

What Artemis III Will — and Will Not — Do

There is a common misconception about Artemis III worth correcting directly: it is not a lunar landing mission.

NASA redesignated Artemis III in February 2026. What was originally planned as the first crewed Moon landing since Apollo 17 in December 1972 is now a crewed test flight in low Earth orbit. The mission will launch four astronauts — commander Randy Bresnik, European Space Agency pilot Luca Parmitano, and NASA mission specialists Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas — aboard Orion on SLS, circularize in LEO using Orion's European Service Module for propulsion, and then conduct rendezvous and docking demonstrations with test versions of one or both commercial lunar landers: SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System and Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman described the restructured mission as analogous to Apollo 9 — the 1969 Earth-orbit test of the Lunar Module that de-risked the Apollo 11 landing. The logic is the same: validate the docking interface, the suits, and the lander systems while still within rescue range of Earth before flying crew into deep space and attempting a surface landing.

The first crewed lunar landing of the Artemis program now belongs to Artemis IV, which NASA is targeting for early 2028. That mission, if successful, will be the first time a human being has stood on the lunar surface since the Apollo 17 crew departed the Taurus-Littrow valley in December 1972 — a gap that will be 55 years.

After NASA's Artemis II crew — Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen — completed a nearly 10-day journey around the Moon and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off San Diego on April 10, 2026, NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya said the program had crossed a threshold. "The path to the lunar surface is open, but the work ahead is greater than the work behind us," Kshatriya said.

The RS-25 delivery is the most recent piece of hardware evidence that NASA intends to walk that path on schedule.

Why the Shuttle Hardware Is Running Out on Purpose

That Artemis III uses the last shuttle-heritage RS-25 engines is not an accident or a supply constraint — it is the plan.

The original 16 RS-25 engines salvaged from the Space Shuttle program were always intended to cover the first four Artemis missions and no more. Unlike on the shuttle, where the engines were carefully removed after each flight, refurbished, and re-certified for reuse, the RS-25 engines on SLS are expendable: they ride the rocket up, detach with the core stage over the Atlantic Ocean roughly eight minutes after liftoff, and are lost to the sea. The shuttle-era stock runs out when Artemis IV launches.

That is where L3Harris's new-production RS-25 comes in.

How Additive Manufacturing Changed the RS-25 — and What It Costs to Save 30 Percent

The new engines maintain what aerospace engineers call "form, fit, and function" parity with the shuttle-era hardware: they bolt to the same mounting points, run the same propellants through the same flow architecture, and produce the same vacuum specific impulse as the engines they replace. But the way their components are built is fundamentally different.

The most dramatic changes involve additive manufacturing — 3D printing for flight-critical hardware. On the heritage RS-25, the pogo accumulator assembly (a beachball-sized shock absorber that regulates liquid oxygen flow to prevent destabilizing vibrations during flight) was built from dozens of separate pieces and joined by more than 100 welds. On the new-production engine, the same component is printed as a single integrated structure. NASA reported that eliminating those welds cut that component's manufacturing cost by nearly 35 percent and reduced its production time by more than 80 percent.

The nozzle jacket saw an even more dramatic redesign. On the Space Shuttle Main Engine, the nozzle jacket required 37 individual components to be fabricated, fitted, and welded together. The new-production version assembles the same jacket from four pieces, using a hot isostatic pressing (HIP) bonding process borrowed from the RS-68 engine program. The main combustion chamber — the heart of the engine, where liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen combust at temperatures reaching 6,000 degrees Fahrenheit (3,316 degrees Celsius) under 3,000 pounds per square inch of pressure — is now built using the same HIP-bonded liner/jacket process.

Across the entire engine, the rigid propellant ducts are now produced using selective laser melting (SLM), an additive process that allows complex duct geometries to be printed directly rather than bent and welded from sheet stock.

The aggregate effect of these changes: L3Harris confirmed the new engines are targeting a 30 percent cost reduction compared with the shuttle-era Space Shuttle Main Engine. That is a meaningful number for a program that NASA's Office of Inspector General found was running billions over budget.

The performance simultaneously goes up. Beginning with Artemis V, all four RS-25 engines on each SLS launch will run at 111 percent of original rated power — two percentage points higher than the Artemis I-IV configuration, and roughly six percentage points above the maximum typical operating level during shuttle operations.

The first of the new-production engines, serial number 20001, completed its full-duration hot-fire acceptance test on June 20, 2025, at the Fred Haise Test Stand at Stennis Space Center in Mississippi. Test teams fired the engine for 500 seconds — the same duration as an actual SLS launch sequence — and ran it up to the 111 percent power level. The second new-production engine, serial 20002, completed a similar acceptance test in November 2025.

L3Harris is targeting a production rate of four engines per year from its Stennis facility — the rate needed to support the annual SLS launch cadence Kristin Houston, President of Space Propulsion and Power Systems at L3Harris, referenced after the Artemis III delivery.

What Happens at Michoud Now

With all four RS-25 engines for Artemis III at Michoud, Boeing will begin mechanical installation and alignment against the engine section of the SLS core stage. That section has been integrated with the core stage tank structures since April 2026, when the upper portion of the core stage was rolled out of Michoud and barged to Kennedy Space Center.

Following structural integration and engine gimbaling system checkout, the completed core stage will be loaded onto the Pegasus barge — NASA's dedicated heavy transport vessel — for a sea voyage along the Gulf of Mexico and up to Kennedy Space Center. There, it will be stacked in the Vehicle Assembly Building with the solid rocket boosters and upper stage components already being prepared for the Artemis III stack.

Launch countdown simulations at Kennedy began in July 2026, and solid rocket booster segments have been mounted to the mobile launcher. The Artemis III Orion spacecraft has an internal readiness target of January 2028, which means the late-2027 launch window — while achievable — remains aggressive.

"This delivery keeps Artemis III on track for launch in 2027," L3Harris's Houston said, "and supports NASA's transition to an annual launch cadence that will enable regular missions to the Moon."

The engines that once helped build the International Space Station and carried John Glenn back to orbit are now pointed, for the last time, at something entirely new.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Artemis III going to land on the Moon?

No. NASA restructured Artemis III in February 2026. It is now an Earth-orbit test mission in which the four-person Artemis III crew — commander Randy Bresnik, ESA pilot Luca Parmitano, and NASA mission specialists Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas — will rendezvous and dock with test versions of SpaceX's Starship Human Landing System and Blue Origin's Blue Moon lander in low Earth orbit. The first crewed Moon landing is now the objective of Artemis IV, targeted for early 2028.

What is the difference between the old shuttle-era RS-25 engines and the new ones being built for Artemis V and beyond?

The new-production RS-25 engines use the same fundamental staged-combustion design and flow architecture as the shuttle-era engines, but key components are built using additive manufacturing (3D printing) rather than traditional fabrication. The nozzle jacket went from 37 pieces to 4. The pogo accumulator — a liquid oxygen shock absorber — is now printed as a single unit, eliminating more than 100 welds and cutting that component's cost by roughly 35 percent. Overall, L3Harris says the new engines cost 30 percent less than the shuttle-era units. They also run at a higher power level: 111 percent of the original rated thrust, versus 109 percent for Artemis I-IV engines, and about 104.5 percent at the end of the Space Shuttle program.

Why are the RS-25 engines on the Space Launch System not reused the way they were on the Space Shuttle?

The Space Shuttle's RS-25 engines were designed to be removed from the main engines after each launch, refurbished, and re-certified for the next mission. On SLS, the core stage — including its four RS-25 engines — separates from the rocket about eight minutes after liftoff and falls into the ocean. Recovering and refurbishing them would cost more than building new ones at the production rates required for an annual launch cadence. The trade-off was evaluated by NASA and deemed acceptable: the new-production engines cost 30 percent less per unit, so the economics of building fresh engines each mission are better than the economics of the shuttle's refurbishment pipeline at the volumes NASA needs.

When will Artemis III launch, and what will it prove for the Moon landing that follows?

NASA and L3Harris are targeting a late-2027 launch for Artemis III. The mission is designed to validate that Orion can successfully rendezvous and dock with commercial lunar landers — systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin that have never before docked with a crewed NASA spacecraft. That demonstration in the safety of Earth orbit is intended to de-risk Artemis IV, which NASA is targeting for early 2028 as the first crewed attempt to land on the lunar south pole since the Apollo program ended.

item.title: What NASA Needs to Stay on Track for the Moon - The New York Times
item.description:
NASA needs many things need to happen before it can try to land humans on the moon in 2028. A timely flight of Artemis III, the third phase in the agency’s moon program, is one of them.

On Tuesday, NASA unveiled the crew of Artemis III and gave an optimistic update on the mission’s status. But it failed to address an elephant in the room: Will Artemis III actually be ready to fly next year?

Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator, acknowledged that the agency has a history of being over budget and behind schedule. “I fully understand the skepticism,” he said in an interview with The New York Times. “We are doing things differently now.”

Much of the readiness for Artemis III depends on Elon Musk’s SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. Both rocket companies are developing landers to be used in future missions to carry astronauts from lunar orbit to the lunar surface. Artemis III will first test critical maneuvers with versions of these vehicles closer to Earth.

Here’s what to know about Artemis III and the milestones that need to be achieved to keep NASA’s moon program on track.

What does the Artemis III mission need to accomplish?

Artemis III is complex: It requires coordinated launches from teams of three mission controllers. NASA will fly the astronauts; SpaceX and Blue Origin will launch their vehicles. The three spacecraft will meet in low-Earth orbit.

item.title: NASA reveals Artemis III astronaut crew - Axios
item.description:
NASA reveals Artemis III astronaut crew

The Artemis III crew. From left: Andre Douglas, Luca Parmitano, Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio. Photo: NASA/Bill Stafford

NASA on Tuesday revealed the four-person roster for Artemis III, the next mission in the space agency's quest to return humans to the Moon's surface.

Why it matters: Artemis III will involve key tests of one or both lunar landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin, in Earth orbit — similar to Apollo 9 before Apollo 11's historic Moon landing.

  • That's after NASA changed Artemis III to a test flight for the landers before a planned Moon landing with Artemis IV.

Driving the news: The Artemis III crew includes mission specialist and first-time astronaut Andre Douglas; mission specialist and record-setting astronaut U.S. Army Col. Frank Rubio, pilot Luca Parmitano (an Italian Air Force colonel and onetime International Space Station commander); and commander Randy Bresnik, a longtime NASA astronaut and former U.S. Marine Corps. colonel.

  • NASA astronaut Bob Hines is a backup crew member who will train alongside the main quartet in case he's needed.
  • All five astronauts involved are male — a departure from Artemis II, when Christina Koch became the first woman to travel beyond low Earth orbit.

The plan: Blue Origin's lander will be launched into Earth orbit first, followed by the four astronauts aboard an Orion spacecraft.

  • They'll rendezvous in space for docking and testing.

Orion will then detach and await SpaceX's Starship for similar docking and testing before the crew returns home to Earth.

  • The two-week mission is set for mid-2027.

What they're saying: "As the first crewed Artemis mission with commercial spacecraft, this test flight will enable us to prove we can carry out highly choreographed operations with our partners across hardware interfaces, software, propulsion systems, and life support elements with crew in the high-stakes space environment," NASA Moon-to-Mars Acting Assistant Deputy Associate Administrator Jeremy Parsons said during a press conference Tuesday.

Reality check: Neither SpaceX nor Blue Origin's landers are ready yet, and the Artemis III mission date could slip.

  • Last month's catastrophic explosion involving Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket also stands to complicate the timeline — though Blue Origin Senior Vice President John Couluris promised Tuesday that the company will be ready to launch in 2027.

NASA's Parsons echoed that sentiment, calling setbacks a "learning opportunity."

  • "We are confident that New Glenn will be ready for Artemis III," Parsons added.

What's next: TheArtemis IV lunar landing is still planned for early 2028 — but any delays for Artemis III could reverberate through the program.

item.description:
NASA will provide an update on the agency’s Artemis III mission and announce the astronauts assigned to the test flight during a live event at 11 a.m. EDT on Tuesday, June 9, at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

The event will stream on NASA+ and on the agency’s YouTube channel. Learn how to watch NASA content through a variety of online platforms, including social media.

Following the event, the Artemis III crew will be available for limited in-person and virtual interviews.

Interview requests must be submitted to the NASA Johnson newsroom by 5 p.m. on Thursday, June 4. International media interested in attending must contact the NASA Johnson newsroom at jsccommu@mail.nasa.gov by 5 p.m., Thursday, May 28. U.S. media must contact the newsroom by 5 p.m., June 4. Registered media will receive confirmation and additional event details by email. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online.

Artemis III will launch four astronauts from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard the Orion spacecraft on the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. The mission will test critical rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial human landing systems needed to deliver astronauts to the lunar surface. Building on the successful Artemis II crewed test flight in April, Artemis III will pave the way for future surface missions.

As part of the Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly complex missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.

item.title: NASA Rolls Out Artemis III Moon Rocket Core Stage - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Following the recent successful test flight of NASA’s Artemis II mission around the Moon, NASA rolled out the core stage, or the largest section, of the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket that will launch the crewed Artemis III mission in 2027. The stage departed from the agency’s Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans on Monday for shipment to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, marking key progress on the path to the agency’s first crewed lunar landing mission to the Moon under the Artemis program in two years.

Using highly specialized transporters, engineers maneuvered the top four-fifths of the SLS core stage, the section containing the liquid hydrogen tank, liquid oxygen tank, intertank, and forward skirt, from inside NASA Michoud to the agency’s Pegasus barge for delivery to NASA Kennedy. After arrival, teams will complete the stage outfitting and vertical integration, and the agency’s Exploration Ground Systems Program will stack the rocket’s components in preparation for launch.

“Seeing this SLS rocket hardware roll out is a powerful reminder of our progress toward returning humans to the lunar surface,” said Lori Glaze, acting associate administrator, Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “This is the backbone of Artemis III. As it heads to Florida for final integration, we are one step closer to testing the critical capabilities needed to land Americans on the Moon, and ultimately, paving the way for our first crewed missions to Mars.”

At 212 feet tall, the completed core stage will consist of the top four fifths of the rocket combined with its engine section. The top four-fifths include the two propellant tanks that collectively hold more than 733,000 gallons of super-chilled liquid propellant to fuel four RS-25 engines. During launch and flight, the fully integrated stage will operate for more than eight minutes, producing more than 2 million pounds of thrust to propel astronauts inside NASA’s Orion spacecraft into orbit.

Building, assembling, and transporting the core stage is a collaborative process for two of NASA’s prime contractors, Boeing and L3Harris Technologies. Boeing is responsible for the overall design and assembly of the core stage, and L3Harris manufactures the rocket’s RS-25 engines. Recent announcements by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman enabled the agency to standardize the SLS configuration, streamline operations, and optimize production to accelerate the Artemis program.

Next year’s Artemis III mission will launch astronauts to Earth’s orbit aboard the Orion spacecraft on top of SLS to test rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial spacecraft needed to land Artemis IV astronauts on the Moon in 2028. NASA’s SLS is the only rocket capable of sending Orion, astronauts, and supplies to the Moon in a single launch.

As part of the Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.
